title: Two merchants
hookLine: Tapussa and Bhallika offer honey-cakes and become the first lay followers

cards: The first customer. Anyone who has opened a shop, started a business, or put something they made out into the world remembers them: the first person who walked in, the first sale, the first stranger who said yes.
You might forget the hundredth. You never forget the first. The seven weeks are nearly over.
The Buddha is sitting under another tree, and he hasn't eaten in all that time, the telling says.
Along the road nearby comes a caravan: carts, oxen, and two merchants from a land called Ukkala, named Tapussa and Bhallika.

teach.b: The brothers see the Buddha under the tree, and something about him stops them.

They come over with the food they carry for the road: barley cakes and lumps of honey, the kind you pack because you don't know where you'll eat next. Please, they say, accept this, for our long good and happiness.
But the Buddha has no bowl, and in the story, a Buddha doesn't take food into bare hands.
So, the telling says, the four great guardian kings of the four directions each appear with a bowl made of stone. He accepts all four, they become one bowl, and he eats.
Then the merchants do the thing that makes them well-known. They go for refuge: to the Buddha, and to the Dhamma, the teaching.
Only two refuges, not the three Buddhists say today, because the third, the Sangha, the community of monks and nuns, doesn't exist yet. There are just two traders on the road.

So Tapussa and Bhallika became the very first lay followers of the Buddha, people who follow the teaching while living ordinary lives with families and work. Before the first monk, there were two merchants.

In Myanmar, a much loved tradition says the Buddha gave them eight hairs from his head as a keepsake, and they carried them home, where they're enshrined in the great golden Shwedagon Pagoda in Yangon.
The first gift the awakened Buddha ever received was a snack for the road, from strangers.

how: Giving (dana) is a foundation of Buddhist practice, and lay Buddhists offer food to monks and nuns daily in many countries; in Myanmar, the Shwedagon Pagoda is honored as enshrining hair relics tradition links to Tapussa and Bhallika.

o: the Buddha's very first lay followers
his first two monks, ordained on the road
two kings who gave him his first bowl

games.q: who gave what — tap the pairs.

s: the first lay followers took three refuges
they took two: the Buddha and the Dhamma. the Sangha didn't exist yet.
the first gift the awakened Buddha received was food for the road
barley cakes and honey from two passing merchants.
they were two traders, lay followers living ordinary lives.

games.q: you're a merchant on a long road. you see a radiant man under a tree who hasn't eaten in weeks. what do you do?
o: keep moving: the caravan has a schedule.
offer him the food you carry for the road.
ask him to bless your trade first.
games.why: they offer barley cakes and honey, he accepts in a bowl from the four guardian kings, and they go for refuge: the first lay followers.

practice: Bring to mind someone you could give a small snack to, a coworker, a child, a neighbor, and picture handing it over: a piece of fruit, a cookie, a cup of tea.
Picture their face as they take it, and notice how the giving feels in your own chest, even imagined. Giving is one of the first things Buddhists learn, and one of the simplest.

wordCard.voice: Two merchants. Tapussa and Bhallika, who offered the Buddha honey-cakes and became his very first lay followers.

orig.note: Pali: a lay follower, literally one who sits near; Tapussa and Bhallika were the first.

carryVoice: Your line: the first gift. A gift, not a trade. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Nidanakatha (introduction to the Jataka): the four bowls and the hair relics
